title: Episode 38: Seward's Folly and the Klondike Gold Rush
description:
In 1867, United States Secretary of State William H. Seward negotiated the purchase of Alaska from Czarist Russia for 7.2 million dollars—less than two cents an acre. Mocked by newspapers as 'Seward's Folly' and 'Johnson's Polar Bear Garden,' the vast frozen territory was vindicated thirty years later when the discovery of tons of gold along the Klondike River ignited an epic stamped of one hundred thousand gold seekers.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In eighteen sixty-seven, the United States was still recovering from the catastrophic devastation of the Civil War. When Secretary of State William H. Seward announced that he had negotiated a treaty to buy nearly six hundred thousand square miles of frozen, subarctic wilderness from Czar Alexander the Second of Russia for seven point two million dollars, the American press exploded with mockery. Editors ridiculed the purchase as 'Seward's Folly,' 'Seward's Icebox,' and 'President Andrew Johnson's Polar Bear Garden.' For thirty years, Alaska was largely neglected, treated as a desolate frozen wasteland. But in July eighteen ninety-seven, a steamship docked in Seattle carrying a ton of pure gold nuggets from the Yukon, triggering the wildest, most grueling gold rush the world had ever seen and proving that Seward had pulled off the greatest real estate bargain in human history. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: MIDNIGHT TREATY WITH THE CZAR
In the spring of eighteen sixty-seven, Czar Alexander the Second of Russia found himself in a precarious geopolitical predicament. Following Russia's humiliating defeat in the Crimean War, the Czarist treasury was depleted, and Russia's far-flung colony in North America—known as Russian America—was a financial drain. With the sea otter population hunted nearly to extinction, the Russian-American Company was losing money, and Russian military planners feared that their British rivals in Canada would seize the territory in any future conflict without Russia being able to defend it. In Washington, United States Secretary of State William H. Seward was a passionate, far-sighted expansionist who believed America's destiny lay in commercial dominance of the Pacific Ocean. When Russian envoy Eduard de Stoeckl approached Seward with an offer to sell, Seward seized the opportunity with electrifying speed. Working through the night by the light of gas lamps at the State Department, the two diplomats hammered out a treaty that was signed at four o'clock in the morning on March thirtieth, eighteen sixty-seven. For the sum of seven million two hundred thousand dollars—roughly two cents an acre—the United States acquired five hundred and eighty-six thousand square miles of land, doubling the coastline of the nation. Russian fur traders had exhausted the coastal sea otter populations and found the remote territory financially unsustainable, leading Tsar Alexander II to propose the sale to Washington following the American Civil War.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE CHORUS OF PRESS RIDICULE AND SUMNER'S STAND
When news of the midnight treaty reached the public, a storm of fierce political satire and ridicule erupted across the American press. Opponents of President Andrew Johnson's deeply unpopular administration viewed the purchase as an outrageous waste of taxpayer money during post-Civil War reconstruction. Influential newspapers like the New York Tribune branded the acquisition 'Seward's Folly,' 'Seward's Icebox,' and 'Walrussia.' Cartoonists drew satirical sketches showing Uncle Sam purchasing caged polar bears, giant icebergs, and fields of snow from Russian diplomats. Critics demanded: Why should the American taxpayer spend millions for a frozen, dark desert where no crops could grow and where no white man could live? Yet Seward, supported by powerful Senate Foreign Relations Chairman Charles Sumner, held firm. In a masterful three-hour speech before the Senate, Sumner documented Alaska's vast natural resources: boundless fisheries of salmon and cod, endless virgin forests of spruce and hemlock, and untapped mineral wealth. On April ninth, eighteen sixty-seven, the Senate ratified the treaty by a decisive vote of thirty-seven to two, and on October eighteenth, eighteen sixty-seven, the Russian double-headed eagle flag was lowered in Sitka, replaced by the Stars and Stripes. Critics in Congress ridiculed Secretary Seward in blistering speeches, claiming that seven million dollars was being wasted on polar bears, walruses, and endless icebergs with zero economic return for the American taxpayer.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THIRTY YEARS IN THE DARK AND THE DEATH OF SEWARD
For nearly three decades following the transfer, Alaska languished in quiet obscurity, governed loosely by the Navy and the Treasury Department. Seward passed away in eighteen seventy-two, never seeing his frozen purchase vindicated during his lifetime. Then, in the summer of eighteen ninety-seven, the world was shaken by an economic earthquake. On July seventeenth, eighteen ninety-seven, the steamship Portland docked at Schwabacher's Wharf in Seattle, having sailed south from the mouth of the Yukon River. Down the wooden gangplank walked sixty-eight weather-beaten, bearded prospectors clad in mackinaws and fur boots, hauling heavy wooden sea chests, buckskin pouches, and milk cans filled with pure gold. The Seattle Post-Intelligencer published a sensational headline that flashed across telegraph wires around the globe: 'Gold! Gold! Gold! Gold! Sixty-Eight Rich Men on the Steamer Portland. A Ton of Gold!' The United States was in the grip of the brutal economic depression following the Panic of eighteen ninety-three; to millions of unemployed workers, bankrupt farmers, and clerks, the news was an irresistible summons to fortune. George Carmack, along with his Native Tagish companions Keish and Kaa Goox, discovered coarse gold nuggets lying like cheese pebbles in the gravel of Bonanza Creek, igniting the wildest gold rush in modern history.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE GOLDEN STAIRS OF THE CHILKOOT PASS
The announcement unleashed the Klondike Gold Rush—the most frantic, desperate mass stampede in human history. Over one hundred thousand people from all walks of life—doctors, lawyers, mayors, waiters, and shopkeepers—abandoned their careers and rushed to Pacific ports to buy tickets on any vessel that could float, from luxury steamers to rotting wooden barges. Arriving at the muddy Alaskan boomtowns of Skagway and Dyea, the stampeders faced the terrifying physical barrier of the Coast Mountains. To reach the gold fields in the Yukon interior, travelers had to cross the Chilkoot Pass or the White Pass on foot. The North-West Mounted Police in Canada enforced a strict survival regulation: to prevent mass starvation in the subarctic wilderness, every single stampeder was required to bring one ton of food and equipment—a full year's supply—before being allowed to cross the Canadian border. This meant that each gold seeker had to haul fifty-pound packs up the sheer, icy stairs of the Chilkoot Pass forty times in freezing blizzards, climbing through knee-deep snow alongside thousands of desperate men in a single-file human chain known as the 'Golden Stairs.' The steamship Portland docked in Seattle carrying sixty-eight miners and more than two tons of pure placer gold, sending an electrifying wave of financial hysteria across an America still reeling from the Panic of eighteen ninety-three.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: DAWSON CITY: THE PARIS OF THE FROZEN PERMAFROST
Those who survived the grueling mountain passes assembled crude wooden rafts and scows from green spruce timber on the shores of Lake Bennett, navigating five hundred miles of treacherous, churning rapids down the Yukon River. By eighteen ninety-eight, an empty swamp at the confluence of the Klondike and Yukon rivers was transformed into Dawson City: the 'Paris of the North.' Swelling to thirty thousand residents almost overnight, Dawson was a surreal frontier metropolis where miners lit cigars with hundred-dollar bills, saloons stayed open twenty-four hours a day, and dance hall girls danced for bags of gold dust. Prospectors worked through the dark subarctic winter in temperatures of fifty degrees below zero, building wood fires on the ground to thaw the permafrost six inches at a time before shoveling gravel out of sixty-foot shafts. When the spring thaw arrived in May eighteen ninety-eight, they washed the gravel in wooden sluice boxes, extracting tens of millions of dollars in gleaming gold nuggets. Fortunes were made in days; a single shovel of gravel from Bonanza Creek or Eldorado Creek often yielded eight hundred dollars in gold. Mounties at the summit of Chilkoot Pass required every stampeders to carry a full year supply of food and equipment, forcing men to climb the Golden Stairs thirty times in subzero blizzards to haul their one-ton outfits.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE NOME GOLD RUSH AND INDUSTRIAL MINING
The Klondike frenzy subsided after just a few years as the richest surface gravels were exhausted and consolidated by industrial mining syndicates. But the prospectors did not go home: instead, they surged west across Alaska to new, even larger gold discoveries. In eighteen ninety-nine, gold was discovered along the sandy ocean beaches of Nome, triggering an astonishing spectacle where thousands of miners rocked gold pans directly in the surf of the Bering Sea. In nineteen oh-two, Italian immigrant Felix Pedro struck rich gold near Fairbanks, establishing the permanent interior capital of the territory. Steamships, river sternwheelers, telegraph lines, and railroads laced the wilderness, transforming Alaska from an isolated frozen territory into a vibrant resource giant. Dawson City transformed in months from a swampy moose pasture into the Paris of the North, where dance hall singers were weighed against pure gold dust on brass saloon scales.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE GREATEST BARGAIN IN HISTORY
Over the next century, Alaska yielded not only billions of dollars in gold, copper, and platinum, but an unimaginable treasure in timber, commercial fisheries, and the colossal oil reserves of the North Slope at Prudhoe Bay. William Seward's seven-million-dollar purchase, once the butt of national jokes, was celebrated as the greatest diplomatic and economic coup in American history. When Seward was asked late in life what he considered his greatest achievement in public service, the old statesman smiled and replied quietly: 'The purchase of Alaska. But it will take the people a generation to find it out.' Today, Alaska stands as America's majestic Last Frontier—a colossal land of glaciers, mountains, and boundless riches, forever vindicating the vision of the Secretary of State who looked at a map of snow and saw an empire. Seward vision proved extraordinarily prophetic, as Alaska yielded billions of dollars in gold, copper, salmon, timber, and oil, establishing the great northern territory as America greatest strategic acquisition.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Seward's Folly and the Klondike Gold Rush remind us that true visionaries are often misunderstood by their contemporaries. It proves that what appears barren and frozen to the short-sighted may hold unimaginable riches for those with the patience to explore. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we witness the heroic dogs and mushers of the 1925 Serum Run to Nome. Until then, stay curious.
